Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] AWS CloudTrail UpdateTrail config tampering (S3 destination swap or validation disabled)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] AWS CloudTrail trail disabled or deleted (StopLogging / DeleteTrail) · [LLM] AWS CloudTrail S3 destination bucket emptied or deleted · [LLM] GCP Cloud Logging sink disabled or deleted · [LLM] AWS CloudWatch Logs group deleted or retention shortened to 1 day · [LLM] AWS CloudTrail log file integrity validation disabled (EnableLogFileValidation=false)
AWS CloudTrail trail disabled or deleted (StopLogging / DeleteTrail) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects an IAM principal invoking cloudtrail:StopLogging or cloudtrail:DeleteTrail, which the article describes as Technique 1 — the most direct way to blind defenders by suspending log delivery to the configured S3 bucket. High-confidence signal: legitimate admin teardowns are rare and usually scheduled. Rationale: Article Technique 1 names the exact APIs (cloudtrail:StopLogging) and impact (no further logs written to S3). Cross-checked AWS CloudTrail API docs and MITRE T1562.008 page — both confirm StopLogging/DeleteTrail as defender-blinding actions. errorCode-absent filter ensures we only alert on successful evasion, not denied attempts (which themselves indicate recon and could be a separate hunt). Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/008/ • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/APIReference/API_StopLogging.html
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1562.008
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Scheduled trail decommission during multi-account consolidation (Control Tower / Organizations migrations)
  • Terraform/CloudFormation stack deletions that own the trail being recreated immediately after
  • IaC drift remediation where a duplicate trail is being cleaned up
  • Disaster-recovery testing in a sandbox account
  • Cost-cutting exercise replacing per-region trails with an org-wide trail
Suppression filter
| where userIdentity.userName !startswith "terraform-" and UserAgent !has "aws-internal"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the userIdentity.arn — is this a human IAM user, a CI/CD role (e.g. Terraform/Atlantis), or an AssumedRole from a workstation? Pull the 24h activity window for that principal in CloudTrail and check for change-control ticket references in userAgent. Step 2 (contain): If unauthorized, re-create the trail immediately and revoke the principal's cloudtrail:* permissions via SCP or inline deny; rotate any active session via sts:RevokeSession. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on sourceIPAddress for any iam:CreateAccessKey, iam:AttachUserPolicy, or s3:DeleteBucket activity within ±1h — StopLogging is almost always the prelude to a larger action the attacker doesn't want logged.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Amazon Web Services"
| where ActionType in ("StopLogging", "DeleteTrail")
| extend TrailName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).requestParameters.name)
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, ActionType, TrailName, IPAddress, CountryCode, UserAgent, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventSource == "cloudtrail.amazonaws.com"
| where EventName in ("StopLogging", "DeleteTrail")
| where isempty(ErrorCode)
| extend TrailName = tostring(parse_json(RequestParameters).name)
| project TimeGenerated, EventName, UserIdentityArn, UserIdentityType, SourceIpAddress, AWSRegion, TrailName, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AWS CloudTrail Logging Stopped or Trail Deleted
id: 3c1f9a6e-2e4d-4f87-9c84-8a73e0b1a9c1
description: Detects cloudtrail:StopLogging or cloudtrail:DeleteTrail API calls used to blind defenders, as described in Unit 42 'Blinding the Watchmen'.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cloud-logging-defense-evasion/
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1562.001
  - attack.t1562.008
logsource:
  product: aws
  service: cloudtrail
detection:
  selection:
    eventSource: cloudtrail.amazonaws.com
    eventName:
      - StopLogging
      - DeleteTrail
  filter_failed:
    errorCode: '*'
  condition: selection and not filter_failed
level: high
source:cloudtrail @evt.name:(StopLogging OR DeleteTrail) @evt.outcome:success -@userIdentity.invokedBy:*
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
fields @timestamp, eventName, eventSource, userIdentity.arn, userIdentity.userName, userIdentity.type, sourceIPAddress, awsRegion, requestParameters.name
| filter eventSource = "cloudtrail.amazonaws.com"
| filter eventName in ["StopLogging", "DeleteTrail"]
| filter not isPresent(errorCode)
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 100
CLOUD
index=aws sourcetype="aws:cloudtrail" eventSource="cloudtrail.amazonaws.com" (eventName="StopLogging" OR eventName="DeleteTrail") NOT errorCode="*" | stats min(_time) as firstSeen, count by userIdentity.arn, userIdentity.type, sourceIPAddress, awsRegion, eventName, requestParameters.name | where count >= 1
AWS CloudTrail S3 destination bucket emptied or deleted AIActions on Objectives High
Detects s3:DeleteBucket (and the preceding bulk s3:DeleteObject) against a bucket that is the configured CloudTrail destination — Technique 2 in the article. CloudTrail's UI surfaces a 'bucket not found' indicator a few minutes after, but by then forensic archive is gone. Rationale: Article Figure 2 caption explicitly shows the CloudTrail console indicator after s3:DeleteBucket; Technique 2 names the exact API combination (s3:DeleteBucket + s3:DeleteObject). The Sentinel join enriches with which trail the bucket served — an analyst doesn't have to look it up at 3am. Cross-checked the AWS S3 API reference and MITRE T1562.008. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/008/ • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/API/API_DeleteBucket.html
ATT&CKT1562.008 T1070.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate trail-bucket migration during account consolidation
  • Terraform destroy on a sandbox account that owned its own trail
  • Lifecycle-policy-driven bucket cleanup when archive moves to Glacier in a different bucket
  • DR tabletop where the trail is being re-pointed at a new bucket
  • Cost cleanup of an abandoned dev trail
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "terraform" and UserAgent !has "cloudformation"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the deleted bucket name against your CloudTrail trail inventory (CreateTrail/UpdateTrail history) — only escalate if it was actively serving a production trail. Pull the past 7 days of userIdentity activity. Step 2 (contain): Revoke the principal's s3:Delete* and cloudtrail:* permissions via SCP; if logs landed in a CloudWatch Logs subscription, switch incident analysis there until S3 is restored from versioning or replicated archive. Step 3 (hunt): Look for s3:PutBucketVersioning Status=Suspended in the 24h preceding the delete (attackers must disable versioning first to prevent recovery), and any iam:CreateAccessKey by the same principal — they often pre-stage egress credentials before destroying logs.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Amazon Web Services"
| where ActionType == "DeleteBucket"
| extend BucketName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).requestParameters.bucketName)
| where isnotempty(BucketName)
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, BucketName, IPAddress, CountryCode, UserAgent, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
let TrailBuckets = AWSCloudTrail
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where EventName in ("CreateTrail", "UpdateTrail")
    | extend BucketName = tostring(parse_json(RequestParameters).s3BucketName)
    | where isnotempty(BucketName)
    | summarize TrailNames = make_set(tostring(parse_json(RequestParameters).name)) by BucketName;
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventSource == "s3.amazonaws.com"
| where EventName == "DeleteBucket"
| where isempty(ErrorCode)
| extend BucketName = tostring(parse_json(RequestParameters).bucketName)
| join kind=inner TrailBuckets on BucketName
| project TimeGenerated, EventName, UserIdentityArn, SourceIpAddress, BucketName, TrailNames, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:cloudtrail @evt.name:DeleteBucket @evt.outcome:success @eventSource:s3.amazonaws.com
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
fields @timestamp, eventName, eventSource, userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress, requestParameters.bucketName
| filter eventSource = "s3.amazonaws.com"
| filter eventName = "DeleteBucket"
| filter not isPresent(errorCode)
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 100
CLOUD
index=aws sourcetype="aws:cloudtrail" eventSource="s3.amazonaws.com" eventName="DeleteBucket" NOT errorCode="*" | rename requestParameters.bucketName as bucketName | join type=left bucketName [ search index=aws sourcetype="aws:cloudtrail" eventSource="cloudtrail.amazonaws.com" eventName IN ("CreateTrail","UpdateTrail","GetTrail") | rename requestParameters.s3BucketName as bucketName | stats values(requestParameters.name) as trailName by bucketName ] | where isnotnull(trailName) | stats min(_time) as firstSeen, count by userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress, bucketName, trailName
AWS CloudTrail UpdateTrail config tampering (S3 destination swap or validation disabled) AICommand & Control High
Detects cloudtrail:UpdateTrail calls that re-point a trail's S3BucketName to an attacker-controlled bucket, disable log file integrity validation (EnableLogFileValidation=false), or replace event selectors to exclude write events. Captures the Continuous Visibility scenario from the article — quietly redirecting the org's logs into the adversary's own account. Rationale: Article's 'Continuous Visibility' section describes attackers transferring logs to their own accounts — a destination swap via UpdateTrail is the cleanest implementation; reviewer feedback #5 calls out validation-disable specifically. Both conditions are rare in legitimate ops because trails are usually IaC-managed. Cross-checked AWS UpdateTrail API doc. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/APIReference/API_UpdateTrail.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/008/
ATT&CKT1562.008 T1530
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Terraform/CloudFormation re-applying with a renamed S3 bucket
  • Security team migrating to a centralized log archive account
  • Compliance team enabling log validation (true) — not malicious; ensure detection filters on false
  • One-time SRE-driven KMS-encryption rollout that re-emits UpdateTrail with the same bucket
  • Org-wide trail consolidation by AWS Control Tower
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "cloudformation.amazonaws.com" and UserAgent !has "terraform"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Diff the new s3BucketName against the inventory of org-owned buckets — if it's a 12-digit account ID you don't own, escalate immediately. Check userAgent for IaC tooling fingerprints. Step 2 (contain): Revert the trail config to the known-good bucket, revoke the principal's cloudtrail:UpdateTrail via SCP, and S3-block-public-access on the rogue destination if it's reachable. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the source account/principal for sts:AssumeRole chains in the prior 24h, and search for the same modus operandi on other trails or on Config recorders (PutDeliveryChannel) — the same playbook applies cross-service.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Amazon Web Services"
| where ActionType == "UpdateTrail"
| extend Raw = parse_json(tostring(RawEventData))
| extend TrailName = tostring(Raw.requestParameters.name)
| extend NewBucket = tostring(Raw.requestParameters.s3BucketName)
| extend LogValidation = tostring(Raw.requestParameters.enableLogFileValidation)
| where isnotempty(NewBucket) or LogValidation == "false"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, TrailName, NewBucket, LogValidation, IPAddress, UserAgent, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventSource == "cloudtrail.amazonaws.com"
| where EventName == "UpdateTrail"
| where isempty(ErrorCode)
| extend Req = parse_json(RequestParameters)
| extend TrailName = tostring(Req.name)
| extend NewBucket = tostring(Req.s3BucketName)
| extend LogValidation = tostring(Req.enableLogFileValidation)
| where isnotempty(NewBucket) or LogValidation == "false"
| project TimeGenerated, EventName, UserIdentityArn, SourceIpAddress, TrailName, NewBucket, LogValidation, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:cloudtrail @evt.name:UpdateTrail @evt.outcome:success (@requestParameters.s3BucketName:* OR @requestParameters.enableLogFileValidation:false)
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
fields @timestamp, eventName, userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress, requestParameters.name, requestParameters.s3BucketName, requestParameters.enableLogFileValidation
| filter eventSource = "cloudtrail.amazonaws.com"
| filter eventName = "UpdateTrail"
| filter not isPresent(errorCode)
| filter isPresent(requestParameters.s3BucketName) or requestParameters.enableLogFileValidation = "false"
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 100
CLOUD
index=aws sourcetype="aws:cloudtrail" eventSource="cloudtrail.amazonaws.com" eventName="UpdateTrail" NOT errorCode="*" | rename requestParameters.name as trailName, requestParameters.s3BucketName as newBucket, requestParameters.enableLogFileValidation as logValidation | eval evasion=case(logValidation=="false","validation_disabled", isnotnull(newBucket),"destination_swapped", 1==1,"other") | where evasion!="other" | stats min(_time) as firstSeen, values(evasion) as evasionType, count by userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress, trailName, newBucket, logValidation
GCP Cloud Logging sink disabled or deleted AIActions on Objectives High
Detects google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.UpdateSink with disabled=true or DeleteSink against a routing sink — Technique 1 / 2 equivalents for GCP described in the article. Sink disable is the exact control the article's Figure 1 console message confirms. Rationale: Article explicitly names logging.sinks.update with disabled=true (Figure 1) and logging.buckets.delete (Technique 2 for GCP); MITRE T1562.008 page confirms GCP sink disable as a sub-technique example. Sentinel KQL left empty because Sentinel's canonical schema in this tenant does not include a validated GCP Cloud Audit table — operators on AWSCloudTrail-only tenants should consume via Datadog gcp.audit or native GCP Security Command Center. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/008/ • https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit
ATT&CKT1562.008
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Terraform run that re-creates a sink (delete + create pair)
  • Project decommission where parent project removes child-project sinks
  • Cost-cutting exercise disabling verbose sinks before quarterly review
  • Folder-level sink supersedes a project-level sink and the redundant one is removed
  • DR drill where logging is being re-pointed to a different log bucket
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Look up the sink name and project; confirm whether it was the org's _Default sink (which captures all admin activity) or a custom-purpose sink. Pull the principalEmail's 24h GCP activity. Step 2 (contain): Recreate the sink from IaC/Terraform state; revoke the principal's roles/logging.configWriter and roles/logging.admin via gcloud projects remove-iam-policy-binding. Step 3 (hunt): Search for iam.serviceAccountKeys.create or setIamPolicy by the same principal in the prior 24h — sink disable usually precedes credential theft or resource exfil the attacker doesn't want exported to Splunk/Chronicle.
title: GCP Cloud Logging Sink Disabled or Deleted
id: 9e2d6b34-1f5c-4d2a-8e74-3b89c1e5a4f2
description: Detects routing-sink disable or deletion in GCP Cloud Logging — Technique 1/2 from Unit 42 'Blinding the Watchmen'.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cloud-logging-defense-evasion/
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1562.008
logsource:
  product: gcp
  service: gcp.audit
detection:
  selection_delete:
    methodName: 'google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.DeleteSink'
  selection_update_disabled:
    methodName: 'google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.UpdateSink'
    request.sink.disabled: true
  condition: selection_delete or selection_update_disabled
level: high
source:gcp.audit (@protoPayload.methodName:google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.DeleteSink OR (@protoPayload.methodName:google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.UpdateSink AND @protoPayload.request.sink.disabled:true))
CLOUD
index=gcp sourcetype="google:gcp:pubsub:message" (protoPayload.methodName="google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.DeleteSink" OR (protoPayload.methodName="google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.UpdateSink" AND protoPayload.request.sink.disabled=true)) | stats min(_time) as firstSeen, count by protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail, protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerIp, protoPayload.methodName, protoPayload.resourceName, resource.labels.project_id
AWS CloudWatch Logs group deleted or retention shortened to 1 day AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects logs:DeleteLogGroup or logs:PutRetentionPolicy that drops retention to 1 day on a CloudWatch Logs group — covers the article's Technique 2 (delete log storage destination) for the CloudWatch Logs delivery path mentioned as an alternative to S3, and reviewer feedback #3. Rationale: Article's Background section names CloudWatch Logs explicitly as an alternative CloudTrail destination, and reviewer feedback #3 calls out DeleteLogGroup/PutRetentionPolicy as the equivalent of bucket destruction. Retention=1 is the lowest the API allows and is functionally equivalent to deletion within the attack window. Cross-checked AWS CloudWatch Logs API reference. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatchLogs/latest/APIReference/API_DeleteLogGroup.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/008/
ATT&CKT1562.008 T1070.007
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dev/test pipeline shortening retention to control costs in ephemeral accounts
  • Lambda function being torn down with its log group
  • Terraform destroy on a stack that owns its own log group
  • Lifecycle automation moving archives to S3 with reduced CloudWatch retention
  • Org-level retention policy reducing per-group retention as part of cost optimization
Suppression filter
| where LogGroup startswith "/aws/cloudtrail" or LogGroup startswith "/aws/guardduty" or LogGroup startswith "/aws/vpc/flowlogs" or LogGroup contains "audit"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Check whether the log group is on the inventory of security-relevant groups (/aws/cloudtrail, /aws/guardduty, /aws/vpc/flowlogs, audit-Lambdas). Anything outside that list is likely benign noise. Step 2 (contain): If security-relevant, restore retention via PutRetentionPolicy and revoke logs:Delete*/logs:PutRetentionPolicy from the principal via SCP. Pull any subscription filters that may have shipped logs to a sibling SIEM — those may still hold a copy. Step 3 (hunt): Look for parallel s3:DeleteBucket / cloudtrail:StopLogging / config:DeleteDeliveryChannel by the same principal in ±1h — multi-surface log destruction is the unmistakable pre-action pattern.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Amazon Web Services"
| where ActionType in ("DeleteLogGroup", "PutRetentionPolicy")
| extend Req = parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).requestParameters
| extend LogGroup = tostring(Req.logGroupName)
| extend RetentionDays = toint(Req.retentionInDays)
| where ActionType == "DeleteLogGroup" or (ActionType == "PutRetentionPolicy" and RetentionDays <= 1)
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, ActionType, LogGroup, RetentionDays, IPAddress, UserAgent, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventSource == "logs.amazonaws.com"
| where EventName in ("DeleteLogGroup", "PutRetentionPolicy")
| where isempty(ErrorCode)
| extend Req = parse_json(RequestParameters)
| extend LogGroup = tostring(Req.logGroupName)
| extend RetentionDays = toint(Req.retentionInDays)
| where EventName == "DeleteLogGroup" or (EventName == "PutRetentionPolicy" and RetentionDays <= 1)
| project TimeGenerated, EventName, UserIdentityArn, SourceIpAddress, LogGroup, RetentionDays, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:cloudtrail @evt.outcome:success ((@evt.name:DeleteLogGroup) OR (@evt.name:PutRetentionPolicy AND @requestParameters.retentionInDays:<=1))
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
fields @timestamp, eventName, userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress, requestParameters.logGroupName, requestParameters.retentionInDays
| filter eventSource = "logs.amazonaws.com"
| filter eventName in ["DeleteLogGroup", "PutRetentionPolicy"]
| filter not isPresent(errorCode)
| filter eventName = "DeleteLogGroup" or requestParameters.retentionInDays <= 1
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 100
CLOUD
index=aws sourcetype="aws:cloudtrail" eventSource="logs.amazonaws.com" (eventName="DeleteLogGroup" OR (eventName="PutRetentionPolicy" AND requestParameters.retentionInDays<=1)) NOT errorCode="*" | rename requestParameters.logGroupName as logGroup, requestParameters.retentionInDays as retentionDays | stats min(_time) as firstSeen, values(eventName) as actions, values(retentionDays) as retentionDays, count by userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress, logGroup
AWS CloudTrail log file integrity validation disabled (EnableLogFileValidation=false) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects cloudtrail:UpdateTrail or cloudtrail:CreateTrail with EnableLogFileValidation set to false — the article's title 'Blinding the Watchmen' captures the intent and reviewer feedback #5 calls this out specifically. Without digest files, log tampering becomes undetectable. Rationale: Reviewer feedback #5 explicitly grounds this: disabling EnableLogFileValidation removes the SHA-256 digest chain that proves logs were not tampered with, precisely the 'Blinding the Watchmen' theme. AWS CIS Benchmark 2.2 and Security Hub PCI.CloudTrail.1 also require this to be true — a legitimate flip to false should be an exception, not the norm. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-log-file-validation-intro.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/001/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1562.008
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IaC drift where the Terraform template was authored before validation was required
  • New sandbox trail created without validation enabled
  • Cost-driven flip during a digest-storage cleanup exercise
  • Migration from CloudTrail Lake (which doesn't use digest files) and someone forgot to re-enable on the file trail
  • One-time compliance evidence-gathering exercise that briefly toggles validation off
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "terraform" and UserAgent !has "cloudformation"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the trail history (DescribeTrails) and confirm validation was previously enabled — a fresh CreateTrail with validation off is lower-severity than a flip on a long-lived prod trail. Identify the IAM principal and userAgent. Step 2 (contain): Re-enable via cloudtrail:UpdateTrail EnableLogFileValidation=true and revoke cloudtrail:Update*/Create* from the principal via SCP if unauthorized. Step 3 (hunt): Search S3 PutObject events against the trail bucket for the 24h window after validation was disabled — any objects placed by a principal other than cloudtrail.amazonaws.com indicate log injection (Technique 5: Log poisoning).
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Amazon Web Services"
| where ActionType in ("UpdateTrail", "CreateTrail")
| extend Req = parse_json(tostring(RawEventData)).requestParameters
| extend TrailName = tostring(Req.name)
| extend LogValidation = tostring(Req.enableLogFileValidation)
| where LogValidation == "false"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, ActionType, TrailName, LogValidation, IPAddress, UserAgent, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventSource == "cloudtrail.amazonaws.com"
| where EventName in ("UpdateTrail", "CreateTrail")
| where isempty(ErrorCode)
| extend Req = parse_json(RequestParameters)
| extend TrailName = tostring(Req.name)
| extend LogValidation = tostring(Req.enableLogFileValidation)
| where LogValidation == "false"
| project TimeGenerated, EventName, UserIdentityArn, UserIdentityType, SourceIpAddress, AWSRegion, TrailName, LogValidation, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AWS CloudTrail Log File Validation Disabled
id: b71c4e5d-3a82-49f8-bd1e-7e2f93a8c5b3
description: Detects UpdateTrail/CreateTrail setting EnableLogFileValidation=false, removing the cryptographic digest that proves logs were not tampered with.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cloud-logging-defense-evasion/
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1562.001
  - attack.t1562.008
logsource:
  product: aws
  service: cloudtrail
detection:
  selection:
    eventSource: cloudtrail.amazonaws.com
    eventName:
      - UpdateTrail
      - CreateTrail
    requestParameters.logFileValidationEnabled: false
  condition: selection
level: high
source:cloudtrail @evt.name:(UpdateTrail OR CreateTrail) @evt.outcome:success @requestParameters.enableLogFileValidation:false
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
fields @timestamp, eventName, userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress, requestParameters.name, requestParameters.enableLogFileValidation
| filter eventSource = "cloudtrail.amazonaws.com"
| filter eventName in ["UpdateTrail", "CreateTrail"]
| filter not isPresent(errorCode)
| filter requestParameters.enableLogFileValidation = "false" or requestParameters.enableLogFileValidation = false
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 100
CLOUD
index=aws sourcetype="aws:cloudtrail" eventSource="cloudtrail.amazonaws.com" (eventName="UpdateTrail" OR eventName="CreateTrail") requestParameters.enableLogFileValidation=false NOT errorCode="*" | rename requestParameters.name as trailName | stats min(_time) as firstSeen, count by userIdentity.arn, userIdentity.type, sourceIPAddress, awsRegion, trailName, eventName
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Vulnerable phoenix_storybook (>=0.5.0, <1.1.0) software inventory for CVE-2026-8467 · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Unauthenticated WebSocket / HTTP 101 upgrade to phoenix_storybook playground routes
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] HEEx / Elixir Kernel injection markers in BEAM-spawned process command line (CVE-2026-8467) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-8467: PhoenixStorybook: Unauthenticated remote code e
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] BEAM / Erlang VM spawns shell or interpreter child (post-RCE — CVE-2026-8467) · [LLM] Erlang .beam compiled module dropped to /tmp, /dev/shm, or %TEMP% by BEAM runtime
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] BEAM process outbound to new public destination or non-standard port (post-RCE C2)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Unauthenticated WebSocket / HTTP 101 upgrade to phoenix_storybook playground routes AIDelivery Medium
Detects external clients negotiating a WebSocket (HTTP 101 Switching Protocols) against phoenix_storybook playground routes (e.g. /storybook/*, /_storybook). This is the article-specific entry point used by the unauthenticated psb-assign event handler for CVE-2026-8467 RCE. Rationale: Article states the playground accepts attribute values 'over WebSocket' from any 'unauthenticated user' and names the affected routes implicitly (story URLs with a Playground tab such as /storybook/core_components/button). HTTP 101 status on these route prefixes is the deterministic pre-exploitation signal. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/phenixdigital/phoenix_storybook/commit/56ab8464d4375fa52db806148a06cce126ad481d
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal developers using storybook for component review from corporate IP space
  • Synthetic monitoring / Pingdom-style uptime probes hitting /storybook/*
  • Internal CI integration test runners that drive the playground UI
  • Legitimate frontend authors live-editing components against staging
  • Browser extensions or accessibility scanners crawling the playground
Suppression filter
| where csUserAgent !contains "Pingdom" and csUserAgent !contains "UptimeRobot" and csUserAgent !contains "site24x7"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the cIP and csUserAgent for the alert. Resolve the cIP — corporate VPN egress / dev workstation / partner is benign; cloud-hosting ASN, residential proxy, or Tor exit is hostile. Confirm whether phoenix_storybook is supposed to be reachable from this network segment at all. Step 2 (contain): If hostile or unexpected source, block the cIP at the WAF/edge and add a deny rule for /storybook* paths from non-management networks. Disable the playground endpoint on prod (`storybook: [playground: [enabled: false]]`) or upgrade phoenix_storybook to ≥1.1.0 immediately. Step 3 (hunt): Within ±5 minutes of the upgrade on the same host, look for beam.smp/erl/erlexec spawning sh/bash/cmd/powershell (UC3), HEEx-marker cmdlines (UC2), .beam writes to /tmp (UC5), and BEAM outbound to non-standard public ports (UC4). Snapshot the BEAM node before restart for memory forensics.
let LookbackPeriod = 7d;
let beamHosts = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackPeriod)
| where FileName has_any ("beam.smp","erl.exe","erlexec") or InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("beam.smp","erl.exe","erlexec")
| distinct DeviceName;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackPeriod)
| where DeviceName in (beamHosts)
| where ActionType in ("InboundConnectionAccepted","ConnectionInboundAccepted")
| where LocalPort in (4000,4001,4002,4003,4004,5000,8080,8443)   // common Phoenix listening ports
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalPort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem startswith "/storybook/" or csUriStem contains "/_storybook" or csUriStem contains "phoenix_storybook"
| where scStatus == 101   // WebSocket upgrade
| where not(ipv4_is_private(cIP))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, scStatus, sPort
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| NOT cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, LocalPort, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

HEEx / Elixir Kernel injection markers in BEAM-spawned process command line (CVE-2026-8467) AIExploitation High
Detects shell or interpreter command lines (spawned by beam.smp/erl/erlexec) that contain Elixir Kernel / EEx / Code.eval markers consistent with CVE-2026-8467 HEEx template injection. The injected expression is compiled via EEx.compile_string and evaluated via Code.eval_quoted_with_env, so System.cmd/2, :os.cmd, Kernel.apply, etc. surface in spawned-process cmdlines. Rationale: Article names the exact sinks (`EEx.compile_string/2`, `Code.eval_quoted_with_env/3`) and the example payload primitive (`System.cmd/2`). The injection breaks out of the attribute string via `foo" injected={EXPR} bar="` — the literal `injected={` token is a deterministic IOC of this specific CVE. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/phenixdigital/phoenix_storybook/commit/e35379dfe2ef1a71b141899e36f431017c55265d • https://github.com/phenixdigital/phoenix_storybook/commit/56ab8464d4375fa52db806148a06cce126ad481d
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer-run `iex -S mix` shell evaluating Code.eval_string against staging
  • Elixir release runtime config (runtime.exs) using Code.eval_string at boot
  • Custom Elixir admin task that legitimately invokes System.cmd from inside the BEAM
  • Mix tasks shelling out via System.cmd during a deploy
  • Test suites driving the playground locally (dev/test env)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "iex" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "mix test"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full ActingProcessCommandLine and the parent BEAM process. If the cmdline contains `injected={` or unmistakable Code.eval_quoted of attacker-controlled strings, treat as confirmed RCE. Cross-check for an UC1 hit (WebSocket upgrade) within 60s on the same host. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host from the network, kill the BEAM node, and rotate any credentials/keys/env vars accessible to the Phoenix release (DATABASE_URL, SECRET_KEY_BASE, AWS keys, OAuth secrets). Upgrade phoenix_storybook to ≥1.1.0 or disable the playground. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all hosts running BEAM for the same pattern over the last 30 days. Pull DNS + outbound NetworkConnects from the BEAM PID for the C2 (UC4). Inspect /tmp, /dev/shm and the release directory for dropped .beam modules (UC5).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("beam.smp","erl.exe","erlexec","beam")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("System.cmd","Code.eval","EEx.compile_string","Code.eval_quoted","Kernel.apply",":os.cmd","injected={")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("beam.smp","erl.exe","erlexec","beam")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("System.cmd","Code.eval","EEx.compile_string","Code.eval_quoted","Kernel.apply",":os.cmd","injected={")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc

BEAM / Erlang VM spawns shell or interpreter child (post-RCE — CVE-2026-8467) AIInstallation High
Detects beam.smp / erl / erlexec spawning a POSIX shell, Windows shell, or scripting/networking LOLBin (sh, bash, cmd.exe, powershell.exe, curl, wget, nc, python). The injected EEx expression executes with full Kernel access so the typical post-exploitation footprint is a child process out of the Erlang VM — which never happens in a healthy Phoenix release. Rationale: Article confirms the injected expression executes with full Kernel access via Code.eval_quoted_with_env/3 — the practical EDR signature is the BEAM VM spawning a shell or LOLBin, which has near-zero legitimate occurrence on a Phoenix prod release. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/phenixdigital/phoenix_storybook/commit/56ab8464d4375fa52db806148a06cce126ad481d
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Mix release start scripts spawning sh during boot (rare, baseline-able)
  • Porcelain / MuonTrap / Erlexec ports invoking helper binaries
  • Health-check probes that exec a shell script from the BEAM
  • Cron-driven Mix tasks that shell out
  • Distillery / Mix release hooks running bash on deploy
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("erl_child_setup","run_erl","mix release") and FileName in ("sh","bash"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm parent ImageFileName is genuinely beam.smp / erl / erlexec and the child cmdline does not match a baselined release-boot or health-check pattern. Pull the BEAM listening port and confirm CVE-2026-8467 affected version of phoenix_storybook in mix.lock. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill BEAM, rotate all secrets in scope of the Phoenix release, and block egress from the host pending forensic acquisition. Patch to phoenix_storybook ≥1.1.0 or disable :phoenix_storybook from the router. Step 3 (hunt): For each affected host, pivot to UC4 (outbound C2), UC5 (.beam drops), UC2 (HEEx markers in cmdline) and audit IIS/nginx logs for the originating /storybook* request (UC1). Search the cluster for the same parent→child pattern across all BEAM hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("beam.smp","erl.exe","erlexec","beam")
| where FileName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","python","python3","perl","ruby")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("beam.smp","erl.exe","erlexec","beam")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","python","python3","perl","ruby")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

BEAM process outbound to new public destination or non-standard port (post-RCE C2) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects beam.smp / erl / erlexec initiating outbound connections to public IPs on ports outside the Phoenix release's normal egress set (HTTP/HTTPS/DNS/SMTP/EPMD). Once HEEx-injection RCE lands the attacker often pivots BEAM into reverse-shell C2 — a healthy Phoenix release rarely speaks ad-hoc TCP to arbitrary public ports. Rationale: Article confirms full Kernel access including Network primitives. EPMD (4369) and the release's documented egress set (HTTPS to APIs, Postgres, Redis) are excluded so the remaining traffic surface is C2-shaped. Sentinel uses an ImProcessCreate→ImNetworkSession join because ImNetworkSession does not carry process-image attribution columns. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-55hg-8qxv-qj4p
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Phoenix release calling a third-party API on a non-443 port (e.g. Stripe webhooks endpoint on 8443)
  • Erlang distributed cluster traffic on a non-default port
  • Outbound to a managed Kafka / RabbitMQ endpoint on its broker port
  • Health-check / metrics push to a SaaS observability endpoint on 4317 (OTLP) or similar
  • Self-hosted Elixir telemetry sink on a custom port
Suppression filter
| where not(RemoteIP in ("<observability-sink-ip>","<managed-kafka-broker-ip>"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Resolve RemoteIP/PTR + Whois. SaaS provider on the release's allow-list → tune. Cloud VPS / dynamic-DNS / Tor exit → treat as C2. Confirm CVE-2026-8467-affected phoenix_storybook present and cross-check for UC1 / UC3 within the last 6h. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, block the RemoteIP at the egress firewall, kill the BEAM node, rotate secrets, patch to ≥1.1.0. Step 3 (hunt): Run the same query org-wide for ≥30d. Pivot to PCAP / NetFlow on the egress edge for the same RemoteIP/port across other internal sources. Search authoritative DNS for any CNAME pointing to the C2 host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("beam.smp","erl.exe","erlexec","beam")
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort !in (80,443,53,25,587,4369,5432,3306,6379)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hits=count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by FirstSeen desc
let LookbackPeriod = 7d;
let beamHosts = ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackPeriod)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("beam.smp","erl.exe","erlexec","beam") or ParentProcessName has_any ("beam.smp","erl.exe","erlexec","beam")
| distinct DvcHostname;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackPeriod)
| where DvcHostname in (beamHosts)
| where NetworkDirection =~ "Outbound"
| where isnotempty(DstIpAddr) and not(ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr))
| where DstPortNumber !in (80,443,53,25,587,4369,5432,3306,6379)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count() by DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol
| order by FirstSeen desc

#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ConnectionDirection=0
| ContextImageFileName=/(beam\.smp|erl\.exe|erlexec|beam)/i
| NOT (RemotePort=80 OR RemotePort=443 OR RemotePort=53 OR RemotePort=25 OR RemotePort=587 OR RemotePort=4369 OR RemotePort=5432 OR RemotePort=3306 OR RemotePort=6379)

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK

| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstSeen max(_time) as lastSeen from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.app IN ("beam.smp","erl.exe","erlexec","beam") AND All_Traffic.direction="outbound" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal" AND NOT (All_Traffic.dest_port IN (80,443,53,25,587,4369,5432,3306,6379)) by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.app, All_Traffic.dest_ip, All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where NOT cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8",dest_ip) AND NOT cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16",dest_ip) AND NOT cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12",dest_ip) | sort - lastSeen

Erlang .beam compiled module dropped to /tmp, /dev/shm, or %TEMP% by BEAM runtime AIInstallation High
Detects beam.smp / erl / erlexec writing a .beam compiled-module file into a temporary or runtime location (/tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm, /run, or Windows %TEMP%). Successful HEEx-injection RCE per CVE-2026-8467 lets the attacker call Code.compile_string / :code.load_binary at runtime — the corresponding .beam artefact landing outside the release's _build directory is a strong persistence/secondary-payload IOC. Rationale: Article specifies Code.eval_quoted_with_env/3 evaluation with full Kernel access — that lets the attacker invoke :code.load_binary on attacker-supplied bytecode, which surfaces as .beam writes outside the release's _build/lib path. A legitimate Phoenix release should not be writing .beam files into /tmp or %TEMP%. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/phenixdigital/phoenix_storybook/commit/56ab8464d4375fa52db806148a06cce126ad481d
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Elixir hot-code-reload / Distillery release upgrade writing temporary .beam files
  • Mix dependency compilation during a deploy that uses /tmp as build root
  • Test fixtures that compile and load a module from /tmp
  • Edeliver / Distillery upgrade tarball extraction touching /tmp
  • ExUnit isolated test environments compiling temp modules
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath has "_build" or FolderPath has "deps")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Hash the .beam file (SHA256) and check against any known-good build manifest for the release. Decompile with `:beam_lib.chunks` / `beam_disasm` and inspect for shell-exec / network primitives. Confirm via cross-correlation with UC2/UC3 within ±10 minutes. Step 2 (contain): Quarantine the .beam artefact, isolate the host, kill the BEAM node before it loads more modules, rotate secrets, patch to ≥1.1.0. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep org-wide for any BEAM-written .beam outside the release _build directory in the last 30d. Yara-scan the artefact across the fleet. Audit `:code.get_path()` and loaded module list on every BEAM node for entries outside the release tree.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".beam"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/run/","\\Temp\\","\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("beam.smp","erl.exe","erlexec","beam")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, FileSize
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType =~ "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "beam"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/run/","\\Temp\\","\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("beam.smp","erl.exe","erlexec","beam")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable phoenix_storybook (>=0.5.0, <1.1.0) software inventory for CVE-2026-8467 AIReconnaissance High
Inventory hunt that surfaces every host running an affected phoenix_storybook release. CVE-2026-8467 is unauthenticated pre-auth RCE — the only durable mitigation is upgrade or disabling the playground, so a clean asset list is the first SOC artefact required. Rationale: Article states 'All versions of phoenix_storybook from 0.5.0 before 1.1.0 are affected' and assigns CVE-2026-8467. A version-range inventory query gives the SOC the asset list for emergency patching before adversaries scan. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-55hg-8qxv-qj4p • https://github.com/phenixdigital/phoenix_storybook/commit/56ab8464d4375fa52db806148a06cce126ad481d
ATT&CKT1518
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • mix.lock in a developer workstation's checkout (not a deployed app, but still patchable)
  • mix.exs in a sample/template repo that's never compiled
  • Pre-release / RC builds of phoenix_storybook 1.1.0 that show as 1.0.99-rc
  • Vendored dependency snapshot in a different project's deps directory
  • Archive of an old project no longer running
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Cross-reference the host list against the CMDB to separate production-serving Phoenix releases from dev workstations. For prod, immediately verify whether the storybook router scope is mounted (`scope "/storybook", PhoenixStorybook.Router do ... storybook_scope/0 end`). Step 2 (contain): Patch phoenix_storybook to ≥1.1.0, or disable the playground in config (`config :phoenix_storybook, playground: [enabled: false]`), or remove the storybook scope from prod router. WAF-deny `/storybook/*` from non-management networks until patched. Step 3 (hunt): For every host returned, run UC1/UC2/UC3/UC4/UC5 for the last 30d to confirm whether exploitation has already occurred. Add the CVE to the vuln-management ticket queue with a 24h SLA.

Pre-auth HTTP.sys integer overflow probe (CVE-2026-47291) AIExploitation Low
Hunts for crafted inbound HTTP requests that may trigger the http.sys integer overflow, paired with crashes or restarts of IIS worker processes (w3wp.exe) or the HTTP service-hosting svchost.exe. Targets the unauthenticated network RCE vector Microsoft flagged as 'more likely' to be exploited. Rationale: Article quotes verbatim: 'unauthenticated attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a specially crafted packet to a targeted server utilizing the HTTP Protocol Stack (http.sys) to process packets'. We can't see the packet shape from network logs alone — the closest behavioural proxy is repeated crashes/restarts of http.sys-hosting processes (w3wp.exe / svchost.exe) correlated with inbound HTTP volume. Low confidence because the same pattern occurs during legitimate worker recycling.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IIS application pool recycling under heavy load (default 29h recycle + memory-based recycles)
  • Web app deployments that restart w3wp.exe several times in a deploy window
  • Health-check probes from external monitoring (Pingdom, StatusCake) inflating inbound HTTP counts
  • Server patching reboots restarting the W3SVC service multiple times
  • Misconfigured load balancers hammering a single backend with retries
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "-deploy-" and DeviceName !has "-stage-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the IIS logs for the affected host in the 10-minute window — examine Content-Length, Range, Transfer-Encoding headers for negative/oversized values. Check System event log for 7031/7034 entries on W3SVC and HTTP services. 2) Contain: if a crafted-header pattern is confirmed (e.g. extreme Content-Length, malformed chunked encoding), block the source IP at the WAF/edge and verify the host is patched for CVE-2026-47291. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP across all internet-facing servers for the same Range/Transfer-Encoding signatures; query DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities for CveId=='CVE-2026-47291' to find unpatched peers.
// Hunt: w3wp.exe / svchost.exe (http-hosting) crashes correlated with recent inbound HTTP — possible CVE-2026-47291 probing
let WindowMinutes = 10m;
let Crashes = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(24h)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "services.exe"
    | where FileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","svchost.exe")
    | where ActionType == "ProcessCreated"
    | summarize StartCount = count() by DeviceId, DeviceName, FileName, bin(Timestamp, WindowMinutes)
    | where StartCount >= 3;  // 3+ restarts of the same http-hosting process in 10m is unusual
let InboundHttp = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(24h)
    | where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
    | where LocalPort in (80, 443, 8080, 8443)
    | where RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | summarize InboundHits = count(), DistinctSrcIPs = dcount(RemoteIP) by DeviceId, bin(Timestamp, WindowMinutes);
Crashes
| join kind=inner InboundHttp on DeviceId, $left.Timestamp == $right.Timestamp
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, StartCount, InboundHits, DistinctSrcIPs
| order by Timestamp desc
// Hunt: http.sys-hosting service restart bursts correlated with inbound HTTP. CVE-2026-47291.
let WindowMinutes = 10m;
let Crashes = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where NewProcessName has_any (@"\w3wp.exe", @"\svchost.exe")
    | where ParentProcessName has @"\services.exe"
    | summarize StartCount = count() by Computer, NewProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMinutes)
    | where StartCount >= 3;
let InboundHttp = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
    | summarize Hits = count(), Sources = dcount(cIP) by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMinutes);
Crashes
| join kind=inner InboundHttp on Computer, $left.TimeGenerated == $right.TimeGenerated
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, NewProcessName, StartCount, Hits, Sources
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\\w3wp.exe OR *\\W3WP.EXE OR *\\svchost.exe OR *\\SVCHOST.EXE) @ParentImage:(*\\services.exe OR *\\SERVICES.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(w3wp|svchost)\.exe$/i ParentBaseFileName=/services\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName], function=count(as=restarts))
| restarts >= 3
ENDPOINT

Malicious RDP server post-connect child process (CVE-2026-42985) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts for child processes spawned by mstsc.exe shortly after a connection to a non-enterprise RDP server — the exact post-exploitation surface for the Remote Desktop Client heap overflows where an attacker-controlled RDP server triggers RCE in the connecting client. Rationale: Article verbatim: 'an attacker who controls a Remote Desktop Server could initiate a remote code execution (RCE) on the machine when a victim connects to the attacking server using the vulnerable Remote Desktop Client'. The detection logic — RDP connection to a non-corporate destination, then a non-baseline child of mstsc.exe within seconds — directly mirrors that attack chain. mstsc.exe almost never spawns non-housekeeping children in benign use, which makes this an unusually clean pivot.
ATT&CKT1203 T1021.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT helpdesk using mstsc.exe to RDP into a customer's home network and launching a remote-support tool locally
  • Developer testing a personal lab over public RDP (rare in well-managed environments)
  • RDP file association launching mstsc.exe with a side-tool (e.g. KeePass auto-type) that races as a child
  • Internal jump-host RDP that egresses via NAT and shows as 'public' RemoteIP in some telemetry
  • RemoteApp seamless windows where mstsc.exe spawns the published app as a child
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIP startswith "10." or RemoteIP startswith "172." or RemoteIP startswith "192.168.") and ChildFile !in~ ("keepass.exe","remoteapp.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the RemoteIP and look up reputation (VT/abuse.ch/internal known-good corp jump hosts). Pull the child process's hash and command line — if it's a known LOLBin or unsigned binary in %TEMP%, escalate immediately. 2) Contain: isolate the device via Defender Live Response, block the RemoteIP at the edge, force password reset for the AccountName if mstsc was launched interactively. 3) Hunt: query DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities for CveId in (CVE-2026-42985, CVE-2026-42992, CVE-2026-44799, CVE-2026-44801, CVE-2026-47289, CVE-2026-48563) across the fleet to find unpatched RDP clients; pivot on the RemoteIP across DeviceNetworkEvents for other connections.
// Hunt: mstsc.exe spawning a non-trivial child after recent outbound RDP — CVE-2026-42985 / -42992 / -44799 client-side RCE
let RdpEgress = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "mstsc.exe"
    | where RemotePort == 3389 and RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | project ConnectTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "mstsc.exe"
| where FileName !in~ ("conhost.exe","werfault.exe","runtimebroker.exe","rdpclip.exe","tabtip.exe","mstsc.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| join kind=inner RdpEgress on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (ConnectTime .. ConnectTime + 5m)
| project Timestamp, ConnectTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ConnectTime), DeviceName, AccountName, ChildFile = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP
| order by Timestamp desc
// Hunt: mstsc.exe child within 5m of outbound RDP to a public IP — CVE-2026-42985 client RCE
let RdpEgress = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where DestinationPort == 3389
    | where ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP) == false
    | project ConnectTime = TimeGenerated, Computer = SourceHostName, RemoteIP = DestinationIP;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has @"\mstsc.exe"
| where NewProcessName !has_any (@"\conhost.exe", @"\werfault.exe", @"\runtimebroker.exe", @"\rdpclip.exe", @"\mstsc.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| join kind=inner RdpEgress on Computer
| where TimeGenerated between (ConnectTime .. ConnectTime + 5m)
| project TimeGenerated, ConnectTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, ConnectTime), Computer, AccountName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, RemoteIP
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @ParentImage:(*\\mstsc.exe OR *\\MSTSC.EXE) -@Image:(*\\conhost.exe OR *\\CONHOST.EXE OR *\\WerFault.exe OR *\\RuntimeBroker.exe OR *\\rdpclip.exe OR *\\mstsc.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/mstsc\.exe$/i
| NOT ImageFileName=/\\(conhost|WerFault|RuntimeBroker|rdpclip|mstsc|tabtip)\.exe$/i
| NOT UserName=/\$$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT

Win32K GRFX SYSTEM elevation chain (CVE-2026-44803/44812) AIExploitation Low
Hunts for SYSTEM-context processes spawned from user-context graphics-rendering processes (dwm.exe, csrss.exe, GDI client apps), or unexpected crashes of these graphics subsystem hosts. Targets the Win32K-GRFX integer-overflow LPE class flagged 'more likely' to be exploited. Rationale: Article specifies the Win32K GRFX subsystem (graphics component) and describes local code execution. dwm.exe and csrss.exe are the canonical user-mode hosts that interact with Win32K; csrss.exe runs as SYSTEM, so a shell descendant is high-signal for elevation. Hunting tier and low confidence because we have no exploit shellcode artifacts — this catches the post-exploit shell, not the trigger.
ATT&CKT1068 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Group Policy startup scripts launched in winlogon context that legitimately invoke cmd/powershell
  • RDP session disconnect/reconnect hooks that briefly chain through winlogon.exe
  • Enterprise UEM agents using csrss/winlogon hooks for kiosk lockdown
  • Crash-dump collectors (WER) that may chain through csrss in edge cases
  • Custom credential providers that legitimately spawn helpers from winlogon
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "winlogon.exe -EmbeddedAutoLogon" and ProcessCommandLine !contains "Microsoft.Management.UI.Console"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm parent process integrity — pull SHA256 of the parent and child binaries; verify whether the host has CVE-2026-44803/44812 patched via DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities. Examine the command line for known LPE indicators (suspended process, token manipulation strings). 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture a memory dump for the child process before termination — Win32K LPE evidence lives in kernel state. 3) Hunt: search for the same parent-child shape across the fleet in the prior 14 days; pivot on AccountName for other unusual elevation patterns.
// Hunt: shell / scripting child of dwm.exe / csrss.exe / winlogon.exe — anomalous, possible Win32K-GRFX LPE chain (CVE-2026-44803/44812)
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("dwm.exe","csrss.exe","winlogon.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe")
| where ProcessIntegrityLevel in~ ("System","High")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          Child = FileName,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          ChildIntegrity = ProcessIntegrityLevel,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// Hunt: shell/scripting child of dwm.exe / csrss.exe / winlogon.exe — possible Win32K-GRFX LPE (CVE-2026-44803/44812)
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any (@"\dwm.exe", @"\csrss.exe", @"\winlogon.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\cmd.exe", @"\powershell.exe", @"\pwsh.exe", @"\rundll32.exe", @"\regsvr32.exe", @"\mshta.exe", @"\wscript.exe", @"\cscript.exe", @"\net.exe", @"\whoami.exe")
| where TokenElevationType in ("%%1936","%%1937")  // Full token / elevation present
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Shell or Scripting Child of Windows Graphics Subsystem Process

references:

source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @ParentImage:(*\\dwm.exe OR *\\DWM.EXE OR *\\csrss.exe OR *\\CSRSS.EXE OR *\\winlogon.exe OR *\\WINLOGON.EXE) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\CMD.EXE OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\\rundll32.exe OR *\\regsvr32.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\whoami.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(dwm|csrss|winlogon)\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/(cmd|powershell|pwsh|rundll32|regsvr32|mshta|wscript|cscript|whoami)\.exe$/i

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("dwm.exe","csrss.exe","winlogon.exe") Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe") by host Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("dwm.exe","csrss.exe","winlogon.exe") Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe") by host Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Hyper-V worker process anomaly — guest-to-host escape (CVE-2026-45607/45641/47652) AIExploitation Low
Hunts on the Hyper-V host for unusual behaviour of vmwp.exe (per-VM worker process) — child process spawning, abnormal crashes, or file/handle access to vmbus device objects — which would indicate a guest VM exploiting the out-of-bounds read vulnerabilities to escape to the host. Rationale: Article verbatim: 'an authenticated attacker on a guest virtual machine (VM) sends specially crafted file operation requests to hardware resources within the VM which could result in remote code execution on the host server'. vmwp.exe is the per-VM worker on the Hyper-V host — it should never spawn shell or scripting binaries, and repeated WerFault[vmwp.exe] crashes are the loudest signal of an in-progress escape attempt. Low confidence as we have no exploit telemetry to anchor on; high value because the FP rate is genuinely tiny on Hyper-V hosts.
ATT&CKT1068 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hyper-V integration services updates that briefly chain through vmwp during VM lifecycle events
  • SCVMM / System Center management agents invoking diagnostic helpers under vmwp
  • Backup software (Veeam, Altaro) hooking into the Hyper-V host for VSS snapshots
  • WerFault crashes during legitimate VM live migration failures
  • Custom Hyper-V scripted automation invoking PowerShell.exe under vmwp
Suppression filter
| where ChildCmd !has "Veeam" and ChildCmd !has "Altaro" and ChildCmd !has "SCVMM"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which guest VM the offending vmwp.exe instance was hosting (the VM GUID appears in the vmwp command line); pull recent Hyper-V-Worker operational event log for that VM. Snapshot the guest VM in-place for forensics. 2) Contain: pause/stop the guest VM (don't shut down — preserve memory state); isolate the host. 3) Hunt: query DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities for CVE-2026-45607/45641/47652 across all Hyper-V hosts; review prior 14 days of vmwp.exe child processes across the fleet for the same shape; check who has guest-VM admin on the implicated guest.
// Hunt: vmwp.exe (Hyper-V VM worker) spawning unexpected children OR crashing repeatedly — possible guest-to-host escape via CVE-2026-45607 / -45641 / -47652
let UnusualChildren = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "vmwp.exe"
    | where FileName !in~ ("conhost.exe","werfault.exe","vmcompute.exe","vmwp.exe")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Kind = "UnusualChild",
              Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
              ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              Child = FileName,
              ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
              SHA256;
let CrashBursts = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName =~ "werfault.exe"
    | where ProcessCommandLine has "vmwp.exe"
    | summarize Crashes = count() by DeviceId, DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, 30m)
    | where Crashes >= 2
    | extend Kind = "CrashBurst", Child = "werfault.exe", ChildCmd = strcat(Crashes, " vmwp.exe crashes/30m");
union isfuzzy=true UnusualChildren, CrashBursts
| order by Timestamp desc
// Hunt: vmwp.exe anomaly on Hyper-V hosts — guest-to-host escape CVE-2026-45607/45641/47652
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has @"\vmwp.exe"
| where NewProcessName !has_any (@"\conhost.exe", @"\werfault.exe", @"\vmcompute.exe", @"\vmwp.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| union (
    SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688 and NewProcessName has @"\WerFault.exe"
    | where CommandLine has "vmwp.exe"
    | summarize Crashes = count() by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 30m)
    | where Crashes >= 2
    | extend NewProcessName = "WerFault[vmwp.exe]", CommandLine = strcat(Crashes," crashes/30m")
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Unusual Child Process of Hyper-V VM Worker (vmwp.exe)
id: 1a4f2e9b-7d5c-4a3f-9c0e-3b6d8e1f5a72
description: Detects non-housekeeping child processes spawned by vmwp.exe on a Hyper-V host. vmwp.exe should only spawn vmcompute helpers, conhost, and WerFault — anything else may indicate guest-to-host escape via CVE-2026-45607 / 45641 / 47652.
references:

source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @ParentImage:(*\\vmwp.exe OR *\\VMWP.EXE) -@Image:(*\\conhost.exe OR *\\CONHOST.EXE OR *\\WerFault.exe OR *\\WERFAULT.EXE OR *\\vmcompute.exe OR *\\VMCOMPUTE.EXE OR *\\vmwp.exe OR *\\VMWP.EXE)

Outlook preview pane → Word type-confusion code exec (CVE-2026-45456/45458/47635) AIExploitation High
Hunts for non-baseline child processes spawned by OUTLOOK.EXE or by WINWORD.EXE when Word is invoked as a renderer by Outlook's preview pane — the explicit attack vector described for the Office type-confusion RCE chain. Rationale: Article verbatim: 'the attack vector is the preview pane of Outlook (classic), and this vulnerability can be exploited when rendering emails in Outlook (classic), as the email rendering in Outlook (classic) utilizes Microsoft Word functionality, where this vulnerability exists'. Detecting non-Office children of OUTLOOK or WINWORD is the textbook hunt for this exact exploitation chain — it doesn't need the user to open the attachment, only for the message to be previewed. The OUTLOOK→WINWORD preview path is the loud signal; we treat WINWORD as a parent too to catch the post-render shellcode child.
ATT&CKT1203 T1566.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Mail-merge macros legitimately invoking external automation (rare; should already be controlled by ASR)
  • User clicking a hyperlink in Outlook that opens a browser → counted because Outlook spawns the browser; mitigate by allow-listing chrome/msedge/firefox/iexplore
  • Add-ins like Adobe Acrobat Connector spawning Acrobat from Outlook
  • Citrix or RDS profile redirectors that wrap Outlook child invocations
  • Corporate signature-management add-ins spawning helpers
Suppression filter
| where ChildFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Adobe\" and Child !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","iexplore.exe","acrobat.exe","acrord32.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the EmailEvents row matching the user/device in the prior 10 minutes — the InternetMessageId + SenderFromAddress + Subject. Hash the child binary; check VT/internal threat-intel. 2) Contain: quarantine the email via Defender for Office 365 ZAP for all recipients of the same InternetMessageId; isolate the device; revoke any session tokens for AccountName. 3) Hunt: query EmailEvents for the same sender/subject across the tenant, and DeviceProcessEvents for the same child SHA256 fleet-wide. Verify CVE-2026-45456/-45458/-47635/-45461/-45463/-45472/-45474 patch state via DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities.
// Alert: OUTLOOK.EXE / WINWORD.EXE spawning a non-Office child — CVE-2026-45456 / -45458 / -47635 / -45461 / -45463 / -45472 / -45474 preview-pane RCE
let OfficeAllowList = dynamic(["splwow64.exe","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","onenote.exe","msoadfsb.exe","werfault.exe","conhost.exe","runtimebroker.exe","microsoftedgeupdate.exe","olk.exe","searchprotocolhost.exe","officeclicktorun.exe","msoia.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("outlook.exe","winword.exe")
| where tolower(FileName) !in (OfficeAllowList)
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "winword.exe" and FileName =~ "outlook.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend SuspiciousChildScore =
      iff(FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","msbuild.exe","installutil.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe"), 5,
      iff(FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\"), 3, 1))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          Child = FileName,
          ChildFolderPath = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256, SuspiciousChildScore
| order by SuspiciousChildScore desc, Timestamp desc
// Alert: OUTLOOK / WINWORD spawning non-Office child — Office type confusion preview-pane RCE (CVE-2026-45456/-45458/-47635/-45461/-45463/-45472/-45474)
let OfficeAllowList = dynamic(["splwow64.exe","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","onenote.exe","msoadfsb.exe","werfault.exe","conhost.exe","runtimebroker.exe","microsoftedgeupdate.exe","olk.exe","searchprotocolhost.exe","officeclicktorun.exe","msoia.exe"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any (@"\OUTLOOK.EXE", @"\outlook.exe", @"\WINWORD.EXE", @"\winword.exe")
| extend ChildBase = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, @"\")[-1]))
| where ChildBase !in (OfficeAllowList)
| where not (ParentProcessName has @"winword.exe" and ChildBase == "outlook.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend SuspiciousChildScore =
      iff(ChildBase in ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","msbuild.exe","installutil.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe"), 5,
      iff(NewProcessName has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\"), 3, 1))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, AccountName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, SuspiciousChildScore
| order by SuspiciousChildScore desc, TimeGenerated desc

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
